cases.input:
Here's a transcript from a talk a friend sent me about using AI coding agents on a TypeScript service. Pull out the rules I should be giving my coding agent.

"Okay so the biggest thing I learned running agents on our billing-sync service at Northwind Labs is that the agent does what the repo teaches it to do. If your repo has three ways of making an HTTP call, you will get a fourth. So we picked one, fetch wrapped in a single client module, and told the agent to always use it. Second thing, tests. Don't let the agent write the test after the code and then bend the test to pass. Write the failing test first, have the agent show it fail, then write the code. We saw so many cases where it would quietly weaken an assertion. Third, small diffs. We ask for one change per commit and we tell it to stop and ask if a change touches more than five files. Fourth, never let it touch migrations or lockfiles without asking, because it will happily regenerate a lockfile and bump forty packages. Fifth, secrets: environment variables only, never inline a token even in a test fixture, use obviously fake values like 'test-token-123'. And finally, error handling. The agent loves to wrap everything in try/catch and swallow the error. We told it: catch only where you can do something useful, otherwise let it propagate, and always log with the request id. That cut our mystery failures a lot. Oh, and one more, we ask it to read the existing file before editing it, because otherwise it duplicates helpers that already exist."
cases.expects: A short Markdown dash-bullet list of unique rules for AI-assisted coding, each a single direct-instruction sentence with no explanations or cosmetic language, covering what the speaker actually said (one HTTP client, failing test first, small diffs, protect migrations and lockfiles, no inline secrets, narrow error handling, read before editing) and nothing invented.

cases.input:
generate code rules from this passage of my draft essay on vibe coding, I want them for my CLAUDE.md:

The thing nobody tells you about letting an AI write your code is that the failure mode is not wrong code, it's plausible code. It compiles, it passes the one test you wrote, and it quietly does something slightly different from what you meant. I started keeping a habit: before accepting anything, I ask the model to state in one sentence what the change is supposed to do, and I compare that to what I wanted. If they differ, the code is wrong no matter how clean it looks. I also stopped letting it add dependencies. Every time it reached for a new package to solve a ten-line problem, I ended up owning a supply chain I did not choose. Now the rule is: standard library first, then what's already in package.json, and only then ask me. The third habit is about naming. Models love vague names like handleData and processItem, and six months later nobody knows what they do, so I make it name functions after the outcome, like markInvoicePaid. Last, I make it leave things alone. If I ask it to fix a bug in parseDate, I do not want it reformatting the file or renaming variables in the next function. Touch only what the request requires.
cases.expects: A dash-bullet list of one-sentence imperative rules distilled from the passage (state intent before accepting, avoid new dependencies in a stated order, outcome-based names, minimal scope of change), without explanation or flourish, and without turning the essay's observations into rules the author did not state.
